summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of the Liberal Party of Australia, covering its anti-socialist founding principles and its historical shifts on economic policy. It traces the party's origins in the United Australia Party (UAP) formed in 1931 under Joseph Lyons, the leadership of Robert Menzies, and the UAP's collapse after the 1943 election. It closes with the party's recent state-level electoral successes in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland.
one_line: Overview of the Liberal Party of Australia's economic stance, anti-socialist founding, UAP origins under Lyons and Menzies, and recent state election wins.
key_facts: The contemporary Liberal Party generally advocates economic liberalism, and historically the party supported more economic protectionism and interventionism than in recent decades.
From its foundation the Liberal Party identified itself as anti-socialist, and strong opposition to socialism and communism in Australia and abroad was one of its founding principles.
Robert Menzies, the party's founder and longest-serving leader, envisaged that Australia's middle class would form its main constituency.
The United Australia Party (UAP) was formed as a new conservative alliance in 1931, with Labor defector Joseph Lyons as its leader.
The newly formed UAP won a landslide victory at the 1931 Election, and the Lyons Government went on to win three consecutive elections.
The Lyons Government largely avoided Keynesian pump-priming and pursued conservative fiscal policy of debt reduction and balanced budgets.
Lyons died in 1939, and Robert Menzies assumed the Prime Ministership on the eve of war.
Robert Menzies served as Prime Minister from 1939 to 1941 but resigned as leader of the minority World War II government amidst an unworkable parliamentary majority.
The UAP, led by Billy Hughes, disintegrated after suffering a heavy defeat in the 1943 election.
Through 2010, the party improved its vote in the Tasmanian and South Australian state elections and achieved state government in Victoria.
In March 2011, the New South Wales Liberal-National Coalition led by Barry O'Farrell won government with the largest election victory in post-war Australian history.
The Liberal and National parties in Queensland merged in 2008 to form the Liberal National Party of Queensland, registered as the Queensland Division of the Liberal Party of Australia.
In March 2012, the Liberal National Party achieved Government in an historic landslide, led by former Brisbane Lord Mayor Campbell Newman.
